label: th-1-1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-1-1}
Let $X$ be a real algebraic
variety (resp. nonsingular real algebraic
variety) and let $Y$ be a homogeneous space for some linear real algebraic
group. Then, for a continuous (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) map $f \colon X \to Y$,
the following conditions are equivalent:
 
\begin{conditions}
\item\label{th-1-1-a} $f$ can be approximated by regular maps in the
$\mathcal{C}^0$ (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) topology.

\item\label{th-1-1-b} $f$ is homotopic to a regular map.
\end{conditions}
head: environment

label: cor-1-2
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-1-2}
Let $X$ be a real algebraic
variety (resp. nonsingular real algebraic
variety) and let $Y$ be a homogeneous space for some linear real
algebraic group. Then every continuous (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) null homotopic
map from $X$ to $Y$ can be approximated by regular maps in the $C^0$
(resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) topology. \qed
head: environment

label: cor-1-3
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-1-3}
Let $Y$ be a homogeneous space for some linear real algebraic group. Then every continuous (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) map $Y \to Y$
that is homotopic to the identity map can be approximated by regular
maps in the $\mathcal{C}^0$ (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty})$ topology. \qed
head: environment

label: ex-1-4
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-1-4}
Here are some homogeneous spaces of interest.
 
\begin{exconditions}[widest=iii]
\item\label{ex-1-4-i} For every nonnegative integer $n$ the unit
$n$-sphere
 
\begin{equation*}
\mathbb{S}^n = \{(x_0, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} : x_0^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 = 1\}
\end{equation*}
 
is a homogeneous space for the real orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(n+1)$. 

\item\label{ex-1-4-ii} Let $\mathbb{F}$ stand for one of the fields $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$
or $\mathbb{H}$. Denote by $\mathbb{G}_r(\mathbb{F}^n)$ the Grassmannian of $r$-dimensional
$\mathbb{F}$-vector subspaces of $\mathbb{F}^n$, regarded as a real algebraic variety
(see \cite[pp.~72, 73, 352]{bib2}). Clearly, $\mathbb{G}_r(\mathbb{F}^n)$ is a
homogeneous space for the group $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F})$ viewed as a linear real
algebraic group.

\item\label{ex-1-4-iii} Denote by $\mathbb{V}_r(\mathbb{F}^n)$ the Stiefel manifold of
all orthonormal $r$-frames in $\mathbb{F}^n$, regarded as a real algebraic
variety. Clearly, $\mathbb{V}_r(\mathbb{F}^n)$ is a homogeneous space for the linear
real algebraic group $\mathrm{O}(n)$ if $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{U}(n)$ if $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}$, and
$\mathrm{Sp}(n)$ if $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{H}$.

\item\label{ex-1-4-iv} Every real algebraic group $G$ is a homogeneous
space for $G$ under action by left translations.
\end{exconditions}
head: environment

label: cor-1-5
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-1-5}
Let $X$ be a real algebraic
variety (resp. nonsingular real algebraic
variety) and let $p$ be a positive integer. Then, for a continuous (resp.
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) map $f \colon X \to \mathbb{S}^p$, the following conditions are
equivalent:
 
\begin{conditions}
\item\label{cor-1-5-a} $f$ can be approximated by regular maps in the
$\mathcal{C}^0$ (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$) topology.

\item\label{cor-1-5-b} $f$ is homotopic to a regular map.\qed
\end{conditions}
head: environment

label: th-1-6
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since each $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $\mathbb{S}^n \to \mathbb{S}^n$ is homotopic to a regular one
(see \cite[Theorem~1]{bib64} for $n$ odd, and \cite[Corollary~4.2]{bib4}
for $n$ arbitrary), the conclusion follows at once from
Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}.
head: environment

label: conj-i
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj-i}
Let $Y$ be a homogeneous space for some linear real algebraic group.
Then, for every positive integer $n$, the set of regular maps
$\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^n, Y)$ is dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^n,
Y)$. In particular, $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^n, \mathbb{S}^p)$ is dense in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^n,
\mathbb{S}^p)$ for every pair $(n,p)$ of positive integers.
head: environment

label: th-1-7
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-1-7}
Let $X$ be a compact connected nonsingular real algebraic variety of odd
dimension $k<2n$. Then a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $f \colon X \times \mathbb{S}^{2n-k} \to
\mathbb{S}^{2n}$ can be approximated by regular maps in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology
if and only if it is null homotopic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Theorem~2.4]{bib5}, each regular map from $X \times \mathbb{S}^{2n-k}$
into $\mathbb{S}^{2n}$ is null homotopic, and hence the conclusion follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}.

let~$k$ be a positive odd integer. If $\dim X = k$, then the set of

label: th-1-9
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-1-9}
Let $M$ be a compact connected $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ manifold of dimension~$m$. Then
there exists an algebraic model $X$ of $M$ such that the set of regular
maps $\mathcal{R}(X, \mathbb{S}^m)$ is dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(X,
\mathbb{S}^m)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Proposition~4.5]{bib4}, there exists an algebraic model $X$ of
$M$ such that each $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^m$ is homotopic to a
regular map. Hence the conclusion follows from Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}.

label: th-1-10
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-1-10}
Let $M$ be a compact connected oriented $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ manifold of
dimension~$m$. Assume that either
 
\begin{iconditions}
\item\label{th-1-10-i} $m \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, or

\item\label{th-1-10-ii} $m \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ and the disjoint union of
two copies of $M$ is an oriented boundary.           
\end{iconditions}
 
Then there exists an algebraic model $X$ of $M$ such that each regular
map from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^m$ is null homotopic. Moreover, a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map
$f \colon X \to \mathbb{S}^m$ can be approximated by regular maps in the
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology if and only if it is null homotopic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion is proved in \cite[Corollary~2.3]{bib41}, and the
second follows from Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}.
head: environment

label: conj-iii
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj-iii}
Let $M$ be a compact connected oriented $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ manifold of dimension~$4k$. Assume that there exists an algebraic model $X$ of $M$ such that
each regular map from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^{4k}$ is null homotopic. Then the
disjoint union of two copies of~$M$ is an oriented boundary.

label: lem-2-2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-2-2}
Any malleable nonsingular real algebraic variety $Y$ admits a dominating
 spray $(E,p,s)$ such that $p \colon E \to Y$ is an
algebraically trivial vector bundle.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $(\tilde E, \tilde p, \tilde s)$ is a
dominating spray for $Y$. Choose an algebraic vector bundle
$\tilde p' \colon \tilde E' \to Y$ such that the direct sum $p \colon E
\coloneqq \tilde E \oplus \tilde E' \to Y$ is an algebraically trivial
vector bundle. Defining $s \colon E \to Y$ by $s(v,v') = \tilde s(v)$, we get a
dominating spray $(E,p,s)$ for $Y$.
head: environment

label: lem-2-3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-2-3}
Let $Y$ be a malleable nonsingular real algebraic variety and let
$(E,p,s)$ be a dominating spray for $Y$. Then there exists a
dominating spray $(\hat E, \hat p, \hat s)$ for $Y$
such that $\hat p \colon \hat E \to Y$ is an algebraic vector subbundle
of $p \colon E \to Y$, $\hat s = s|_{\hat
E}$, and the restriction
 
\begin{equation*}
d_{0_y} \hat s|_{\hat E_y} \colon \hat E_y \to T_y Y
\end{equation*}
 
of the derivative $d_{0_y} \hat s \colon T_{0_y} \hat E \to T_y Y$ is a
linear isomorphism for all $y \in Y$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha \colon E \to TY$ be the morphism of algebraic vector bundles
over $Y$ defined by
 
\begin{equation*}
\alpha(v) = d_{0_{p(v)}} s(v) \quad \text{for all } v \in E.
\end{equation*}
 
Since $\alpha$ is a surjective morphism, its kernel $\operatorname{Ker} \alpha$ is an
algebraic vector subbundle of $E$. It follows that $E = \hat E \oplus
\operatorname{Ker} \alpha$ is the direct sum for some algebraic vector subbundle $\hat
p \colon \hat E \to Y$ of $p \colon E \to Y$. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: prop-2-4
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-2-4}
Any malleable nonsingular real algebraic variety $Y$ admits a
dominating spray of the form $(TY, \pi,  \sigma)$, where
$\pi \colon TY \to Y$ is the tangent bundle to $Y$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
With notation as in Lemma~\ref{lem-2-3}, the vector bundle $\hat E$ is
isomorphic to the tangent bundle $TY$, which completes the proof.

label: ex-2-5
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-2-5}
Let $G$ denote either the real orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(n)$ or the real
special orthogonal group $\mathrm{SO}(n)$. Then each homogeneous space $Y$ for
$G$ is malleable. This assertion can be established by direct
computation as follows.

Let $\mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ be the $\mathbb{R}$-algebra of all $n$-by-$n$
matrices with real entries. Let $0$~and~$1$ stand for the zero matrix
and the identity matrix in $\mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbb{R})$. Using the determinant function
$\det$, we obtain a Zariski open neighborhood
 
\begin{equation*}
\Omega \coloneqq \{ x \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbb{R}) : \det(1+x) \neq 0 \}
\end{equation*}
 
of the zero matrix. We identify the tangent space to $G$ at $1$ with the
vector subspace $V$ of $\mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbb{R})$ comprising all skew symmetric
matrices; $V \cong \mathbb{R}^d$ where $d = n(n-1)/2$. Thus
 
\begin{equation*}
\varphi \colon V \to G \cap \Omega, \quad v \mapsto (1-v)(1+v)^{-1}
\end{equation*}
 
is a well-defined biregular isomorphism with $\varphi(0)=1$. 
We get a dominating
spray $(E,p,s)$ for $Y$, where $p \colon E \coloneqq Y \times V \to
Y$ is the product vector bundle and $s \colon E
\to Y$ is defined by $s(y,v) = \varphi(v) \cdot y$ for all $(y,v) \in
E$.

label: prop-2-8
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-2-8}
Let $G$ be a linear real algebraic group. Then each homogeneous space~$Y$ for $G$ is a malleable variety.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d = \dim G$ and let $G^0$ be the irreducible component of the
variety $G$ that contains the identity element $1$ of $G$. By a theorem
of Chevalley \cite[Theorem~2]{bib24} or \cite[Corollary~7.12]{bib19},
$G^0$ is a unirational variety, and hence there exist a Zariski open
subset~$U$ of~$\mathbb{R}^d$ and a regular map $\psi \colon U \to G^0$ such that
the image $\psi(U)$ is Zariski dense in $G^0$. Clearly, at some point $a
\in U$ the derivative $d_a \psi \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to T_{\psi(a)} G^0$ is a
linear isomorphism. Using a translation in $\mathbb{R}^d$ we may assume that
$a=0 \in U$. The map $\varphi \colon U \to G$, $v \mapsto
\psi(v)\psi(0)^{-1}$ is regular, $\varphi(0) = 1$, and the derivative of
$\varphi$ at $0$ is a linear isomorphism. As noted by J\'anos Koll\'ar in no.~\ref{Kollar-2} of the Appendix, taking the map
 
\begin{equation*}
    h \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, \quad h(v) = \frac{cv}{1+\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}}{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}*}}{\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}}{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}*}*}}{\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}}{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}*}}{\@ifstar{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}}{\@ifstar{\norm}{\norm*}*}*}*}{v}^2},
\end{equation*}
 
where $c$ is a small positive real number, we obtain a regular map $g \coloneqq \varphi \circ h \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to G$ such that $g(0)=1$ and the derivative of $g$ at $0$ is a linear isomorphism. 
Now we obtain a~dominating spray $(E,p,s)$ for $Y$, where $p \colon E \coloneqq Y
\times \mathbb{R}^d \to Y$ is the product vector bundle 
and $s \colon E \to Y$ is defined by $s(y,v) = g(v) \cdot y$ for
all $(y,v) \in E$.

label: lem-3-3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-3-3}
If the submersion $h\colon Z \to X$ is malleable, then it admits a
dominating spray $(E,p,s)$ such that $p \colon E \to Z$ is
an algebraically trivial vector bundle.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $(\tilde E, \tilde p, \tilde s)$ is a
dominating spray for $h \colon Z \to X$. Choose an algebraic
vector bundle $\tilde p' \colon \tilde E' \to Z$ such that the direct
sum $p \colon E \coloneqq \tilde E \oplus \tilde E' \to Z$ is an
algebraically trivial vector bundle. Defining $s \colon E \to Z$ by $s(v,v') = \tilde s(v)$, we get a
dominating spray $(E,p,s)$ for $h \colon Z \to X$.
head: environment

label: lem-3-4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-3-4}
Suppose that $(E,p,s)$ is a dominating spray for the
submersion $h \colon Z \to X$. Then there exists a dominating
spray $(\hat E, \hat p, , \hat s)$ for $h \colon Z \to X$ such
that $\hat p \colon \hat E \to Z$ is an algebraic vector subbundle of $p
\colon E \to Z$, $\hat s = s|_{\hat E}$,
and the restriction
 
\begin{equation*}
d_{0_z} \hat s|_{\hat E_z} \colon \hat E_z \to V(h)_z
\end{equation*}
 
of the derivative $d_{0_z} \hat s \colon T_{0_z} \hat E \to T_z Z$ is a
linear isomorphism for all $z \in Z$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha \colon E \to V(h)$ be a morphism of algebraic vector bundles
over $Z$ defined by
 
\begin{equation*}
\alpha(v) = d_{0_{p(v)}} s(v) \quad \text{for all } v \in E.
\end{equation*}
 
Since $\alpha$ is a surjective morphism, its kernel $\operatorname{Ker} \alpha$ is an
algebraic vector subbundle of~$E$. It follows that $E = \hat E \oplus
\operatorname{Ker} \alpha$ is the direct sum for some algebraic vector subbundle $\hat
p \colon \hat E \to Z$ of $p \colon E \to Z$. This completes the proof.

label: lem-3-6
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x \in U$. The zero vector in the fiber $(E_f)_x$ is $(x,
0_{f(x)})$, where $0_{f(x)}$ is the zero vector in the fiber
$E_{f(x)}$. Since $s_f(x,0_{f(x)}) = s(0_{f(x)}) = f(x)$, it follows
that $s_f$ induces a diffeomorphism between $Z(E_f)$ and $f(U)$.
Moreover, the derivative
 
\begin{equation*}
d_{(x, 0_{f(x)})} s_f \colon T_{(x, 0_{f(x)})} E_f \to T_{f(x)}Z
\end{equation*}
 
is an isomorphism because
 
\begin{equation*}
d_{0_z} s|_{E_z} \colon E_z \to V(h)_z
\end{equation*}
 
is an isomorphism for all $z \in Z$. Consequently, $s_f$ is a local
diffeomorphism at the point $(x,0_{f(x)})$. Now the lemma follows from \cite[(12.7)]{bib23}.
head: environment

label: lem-3-7
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-3-7}
Suppose that $(E, p, s)$ is a dominating spray for the
submersion $h \colon Z \to X$. Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$ and let
$F \colon U \times [0,1] \to Z$ be a homotopy of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections of
$h \colon Z \to X$. Let $U_0$ be an open subset of $X$ whose closure
$\overline{U_0}$ is compact and contained in $U$. Let $t_0$ be a point
in $[0,1]$. Then there exist a neighborhood $I_0$ of $t_0$ in $[0,1]$
and a continuous map $\xi \colon U_0 \times I_0 \to E$ such that
 
\begin{inthm}[widest=3.7.2]
\item\label{lem-3-7-1} $p(\xi(x,t)) = F(x,t_0)$ for all $(x,t) \in U_0
\times I_0$,

\item\label{lem-3-7-2} $\xi(x,t_0) = 0_{F(x,t_0)}$ for all $x \in U_0$,

\item\label{lem-3-7-3} $s(\xi(x,t)) = F(x,t)$ for all $(x,t) \in U_0
\times I_0$,

\item\label{lem-3-7-4} for every $t \in I_0$ the map $U_0 \to E^0$, $x
\mapsto \xi(x,t)$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$.
\end{inthm}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem-3-4}, we may assume without loss of generality that
 
\begin{equation*}
d_{0_z}s|_{E_z} \colon E_z \to V(h)_z
\end{equation*}
 
is an isomorphism for all $z \in Z$. Defining $f \colon U \to Z$ by
$f(x) = F(x, t_0)$, in view of Lemma~\ref{lem-3-6}, there exist an open
neighborhood $M \subseteq E_f$ of the zero section $Z(E_f)$ and an
open neighborhood $N \subseteq Z$ of $f(U)$ such that the restriction
$\sigma \colon M \to N$ of $s_f \colon E_f \to Z$ is a diffeomorphism.
Since $\overline{U_0}$ is a compact subset of $U$, we can choose an open
neighborhood~$I_0$ of $t_0$ in $[0,1]$ such that $F_t(U_0) \subseteq N$
for all $t \in I_0$. Therefore, for each $t \in I_0$, there exists a
unique $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $\zeta_t \colon U_0 \to E_f$ satisfying
$\zeta_t(U_0) \subseteq M$ and $F_t(x) = \sigma(\zeta_t(x))$ for all $x
\in U_0$. Writing $\zeta_t(x)$ as $\zeta_t(x) = (\alpha_t(x),
\xi_t(x))$, where $\alpha_t \colon U_0 \to U$ and $\xi_t \colon U_0 \to
E$ are $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps, we get
 
\begin{equation*}
f(\alpha_t(x)) = p(\xi_t(x)) \quad \text{and} \quad s(\xi_t(x)) =
F_t(x).
\end{equation*}
 
By Definition~\ref{def-3-2}\ref{def-3-2-i}, $s(\xi_t(x)) \in
h^{-1}(h(p(\xi_t(x))))$, and hence
 
\begin{equation*}
h(s(\xi_t(x))) = h(f(\alpha_t(x))) = \alpha_t(x).
\end{equation*}
 
On the other hand,
 
\begin{equation*}
h(s(\xi_t(x))) = h(F_t(x)) = x.
\end{equation*}
 
Consequently, $\alpha_t(x)=x$. It follows that $\zeta_t \colon U_0 \to
E_f$ is a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ section, over $U_0$, of the vector bundle $p_f
\colon E_f \to U$. Clearly, $\zeta_{t_0}(U_0) \subseteq Z(E_f)$.
Furthermore, the map
 
\begin{equation*}
\zeta \colon U_0 \times I_0 \to E_f, \quad (x,t) \mapsto \zeta_t(x)
\end{equation*}
 
is continuous. Note that $\zeta(x,t) = (x,\xi(x,t))$, where
 
\begin{equation*}
\xi \colon U_0 \times I_0 \to E, \quad (x,t) \mapsto \xi_t(x)
\end{equation*}
 
is a continuous map with $p(\xi(x,t)) = f(x) = F(x,t_0)$ for all $(x,t)
\in U_0 \times I_0$. By construction, the map~$\xi$ satisfies conditions
\ref{lem-3-7-1}--\ref{lem-3-7-4}.

label: lem-3-8
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-3-8}
Assume that the submersion $h \colon Z \to X$ is malleable. Let $U$ be
an open subset of $X$ and let $F \colon U \times [0,1] \to Z$ be a
homotopy of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections of $h \colon Z \to X$. Let $U_0$ be an
open subset of $X$ whose closure $\overline{U_0}$ is compact and
contained in $U$. Then there exist a dominating spray
$(E,p,s)$ for $h \colon Z \to X$ and a continuous map $\xi \colon
U_0 \times [0,1] \to E$ such that $p \colon E = Z \times \mathbb{R}^n \to Z$
is the product vector bundle and $\xi(x,t) = (F(x,0), \eta(x,t))$ for
all $(x,t) \in U_0 \times [0,1]$, where the map $\eta \colon U_0 \times
[0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies
 
\begin{inthm}[widest=3.8.3]
\item\label{lem-3-8-1} $\eta(x,0)=0$ for all $x \in U_0$,

\item\label{lem-3-8-2} $s(F(x,0),\eta(x,t)) = F(x,t)$ for all $(x,t) \in
U_0 \times [0,1]$,

\item\label{lem-3-8-3} for every $t \in [0,1]$ the map $U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^n$,
$x \mapsto \eta(x,t)$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$.
\end{inthm}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem-3-3}, the submersion $h \colon Z \to X$ admits a
dominating spray $(\tilde E, \tilde p, \tilde s)$
such that $\tilde p \colon \tilde E = Z \times \mathbb{R}^m \to Z$ is the product
vector bundle. In view of Lemma~\ref{lem-3-7} and the compactness of the
interval $[0,1]$ (see the Lebesgue lemma for compact metric spaces
\cite[p.~28, Lemma~9.11]{bib22}), there exists a partition $0=t_0 < t_1
< \cdots < t_k =1$ of $[0,1]$ such that for each $i=1,\ldots,k$ there
exists a continuous map $\xi^i \colon U_0 \times [t_{i-1},t_i] \to \tilde
E$ with the following properties:
 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\xi^i(x,t) = (F(x,t_{i-1}), \eta^i(x,t))$ for all $(x,t) \in U_0
\times [t_{i-1},t_i]$,

\item $\eta^i(x, t_{i-1}) = 0$ for all $x \in U_0$,

\item $\tilde s(F(x,t_{i-1}), \eta^i(x,t)) = F(x,t)$ for all $(x,t) \in
U_0 \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]$,

\item for every $t \in [t_{i-1}, t_i]$ the map $U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^m$, $x
\mapsto \eta^i(x,t)$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$.
\end{itemize}
 
For $i=1,\ldots,k$ we define recursively a dominating spray
$(E(i), p^{(i)}, s^{(i)})$ for $h \colon Z \to X$ by
 
\begin{equation*}
(E(i), p^{(i)}, s^{(i)}) = (\tilde E, \tilde p,\tilde s) \quad \text{if } i=1,
\end{equation*}
 
while for $i \geq 2$ we require
 
\begin{equation*}
p^{(i)} \colon E(i) = Z \times (\mathbb{R}^m)^i \to Z
\end{equation*}
 
to be the product vector bundle and set
 
\begin{equation*}
s^{(i)} \colon E(i) \to Z, \quad s^{(i)}(z, v_1,\ldots,v_i) =
s^{(1)}(s^{(i-1)}(z, v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}), v_i),
\end{equation*}
 
where $z \in Z$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_i \in \mathbb{R}^m$.

In particular, $(E,p,s) \coloneqq (E(k), p^{(k)}, s^{(k)})$
is a dominating spray for $h \colon Z \to X$. Note that $p
\colon E = Z \times \mathbb{R}^n \to Z$ is the product vector bundle with $\mathbb{R}^n
= (\mathbb{R}^m)^k$. Now, consider a map
 
\begin{equation*}
\xi \colon U_0 \times [0,1] \to E, \quad \xi(x,t) = (F(x,0),
\eta(x,t)),
\end{equation*}
 
where $\eta \colon U_0 \times [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^n = (\mathbb{R}^m)^k$ is defined by
 
\begin{equation*}
\eta(x,t) = (\eta^1(x,t), 0,\ldots,0)
\end{equation*}
 
for all $(x,t) \in U_0 \times [t_0,t_1]$, and
 
\begin{equation*}
\eta(x,t) = (\eta^1(x,t_1), \ldots, \eta^{i-1}(x,t_{i-1}), \eta^i(x,t),
0,\ldots, 0)
\end{equation*}
 
for all $(x,t) \in U_0 \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]$ with $i=2,\ldots,k$. One
readily checks that $\eta$ is a well-defined continuous map satisfying
\ref{lem-3-8-1}--\ref{lem-3-8-3}.

label: th-3-9
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-3-9}
Assume that the submersion $h \colon Z \to X$ is malleable. Let $U$ be
an open subset of $X$ and let $f \colon U \to Z$ be a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ section
of $h \colon Z \to X$ that is homotopic through $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections to a
regular section. Then 
$f$ can be approximated by regular sections of $h
\colon Z \to X$ in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F \colon U \times [0,1] \to Z$ be a homotopy of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections
such that $F_0$ is a regular section and $F_1 = f$. Let $U_0$ be an open
subset of $X$ such that its closure $\overline{U_0}$ is compact
and contained in $U$,
and let $(E,p,s)$, $\xi \colon U_0 \times [0,1] \to E$, $\xi(x,t)
= (F(x,0), \eta(x,t))$, ${\eta \colon U_0 \times [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^n}$ be as in
Lemma~\ref{lem-3-8}. In particular, we have
 
\begin{equation*}
s(F(x,0), \eta(x,1)) = F(x,1) = f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in U_0.
\end{equation*}
 
By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, there exists a regular map $\beta \colon X \to \mathbb{R}^n$ such that the restriction $\beta|_{U_0}$ is arbitrarily close to the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $\eta_1 \colon U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \mapsto \eta(x,1)$ in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology. Then
 
\begin{equation*}
    g \colon U \to Z, \quad x \mapsto s(F(x,0), \beta(x))
\end{equation*}
 
is a regular map such that $g|_{U_0}$ is close to $f|_{U_0}$ in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology. Moreover, in view of Definition~\ref{def-3-2}\ref{def-3-2-i}, $g \colon U \to Z$ is a section of $h \colon Z \to X$. The proof is complete since $U_0$ is chosen in an arbitrary way.
head: environment

label: cor-3-10
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-3-10}
Assume that the submersion $h \colon Z \to X$ is malleable. Let $f \colon X \to Z$ be a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ section of
$h \colon Z \to X$ that is homotopic through $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections to a
regular section. Then $f$ can be approximated by regular sections of $h
\colon Z \to X$ in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology. \qed

label: lem-4-1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(E,p,s)$ be a dominating spray for $Y$. We obtain a
dominating spray $(\tilde E, \tilde p, \tilde s)$
for $h \colon X \times Y \to X$ setting
 
\begin{align*}
&\tilde E = \{ ((x,y),v) \in (X \times Y) \times E : y=p(v)\},\\
 
&\tilde p \colon \tilde E \to X \times Y, \quad ((x,y),v) \mapsto
(x,y),\\
 
&\tilde s \colon \tilde E \to X \times Y, \quad ((x,y),v) \mapsto
(x,s(v)).\qedhere
\end{align*}

label: th-4-2
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove \ref{th-4-2-b}$\Rightarrow$\ref{th-4-2-a}. To this
end let $\Phi \colon X \times [0,1] \to Y$ be a homotopy such that
$\Phi_0$ is a regular map and $\Phi_1=f$. We may assume that $\Phi$ is a
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map, see \cite[Proposition~10.22]{bib49a}. By
Lemma~\ref{lem-4-1}, the canonical projection $h \colon X \times Y \to
X$ is a malleable submersion. Clearly,
 
\begin{equation*}
F \colon X \times [0,1] \to X \times Y, \quad (x,t) \mapsto (x,
\Phi(x,t))
\end{equation*}
 
is a homotopy of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections of $h \colon X \times Y \to X$.
Therefore, according to Corollary~\ref{cor-3-10}, the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ section
 
\begin{equation*}
X \to X \times Y, \quad x \mapsto (x,f(x))
\end{equation*}
 
can be approximated by regular sections in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology, which
implies that \ref{th-4-2-a} holds.
head: environment

label: th-4-3
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove \ref{th-4-3-b}$\Rightarrow$\ref{th-4-3-a}. Suppose
that \ref{th-4-3-b} holds, and let $\gamma \colon X \to Y$ be a regular map
homotopic to $f$. We may assume that $X,Y$ are Zariski closed subsets of
$\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^l$, respectively. Then there exists a Zariski open neighborhood
$\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ of $X$ and a regular map $\tilde \gamma \colon \Omega
\to \mathbb{R}^l$ with $\tilde \gamma|_X = \gamma$, see \cite[p.~62]{bib2}. By the Tietze
extension theorem, there exists a continuous map $\tilde f \colon \Omega
\to \mathbb{R}^l$ with $\tilde f|_X = f$. Now, let $\rho \colon T \to Y$ be a
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ tubular neighborhood of $Y$ in $\mathbb{R}^l$, where $T$ is an open
neighborhood of $Y$ in $\mathbb{R}^l$ and $\rho$ is a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ retraction.
Choose an open neighborhood $U \subseteq \Omega$ of $X$ such that
$\tilde f(U) \subseteq T$ and $\tilde \gamma(U) \subseteq T$. By \cite[p.~44, Theorem~2.2]{bib32}, we can also
choose a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $U \to T$ arbitrarily close to $\tilde f|_U
\colon U \to T$ in the strong $\mathcal{C}^0$ topology; 
such a map is homotopic to $\tilde f|_U \colon U \to T$. Therefore, for
the proof of \ref{th-4-3-a}, we may assume that the map $\tilde f|_U
\colon U \to T$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$. Clearly, the maps $\varphi, \psi
\colon U \to Y$, defined by
 
\begin{equation*}
\varphi(x) = \rho(\tilde \gamma(x)), \quad \psi(x) = \rho(\tilde f(x)) \quad
\text{for all } x \in U,
\end{equation*}
 
are of class $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ and satisfy $\varphi|_X=\gamma$, $\psi|_X=f$.
Shrinking $U$, the variety $X$ is a continuous retract of $U$
($X$ is locally contractible \cite[Theorem~9.3.6]{bib2}, so it is a Euclidean neighborhood retract by Borsuk's theorem \cite[p.~537, Theorem~E.3]{bib22}).
Consequently, the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\varphi, \psi$ are homotopic, and hence
there exists a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ homotopy $\Phi \colon U \times [0,1] \to Y$
with $\Phi_0 = \varphi$ and $\Phi_1 = \psi$ \cite[Proposition~10.22]{bib49a}. Let $U_0 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be
an open subset whose closure $\overline{U_0}$ is compact
and contained in $U$.

Consider the canonical projection $h \colon \mathbb{R}^k \times Y \to \mathbb{R}^k$ and
the homotopy of its $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ sections
 
\begin{equation*}
F \colon U \to \mathbb{R}^k \times Y, \quad x \mapsto (x,\Phi(x,t)).
\end{equation*}
 
According to Lemma~\ref{lem-4-1}, $h \colon \mathbb{R}^k \times Y \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is a
malleable submersion. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem-3-8}, there exist a
dominating spray $(E,p,s)$ for $h \colon \mathbb{R}^k \times Y \to
\mathbb{R}^k$ and a continuous map ${\xi \colon U_0 \times [0,1] \to E}$ such that
$p \colon E = (\mathbb{R}^k \times Y) \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k \times Y$ is the
product vector bundle and $\xi(x,t) = (F(x,0), \eta(x,t))$, where the
continuous map $\eta \colon U_0 \times [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies
 
\begin{equation*}
s(F(x,0), \eta(x,t)) = F(x,t) \quad \text{for all } (x,t) \in U_0 \times
[0,1].
\end{equation*}
 
In particular,
 
\begin{equation*}
s(F(x,0), \eta(x,1)) = F(x,1) = (x, \psi(x)) \quad \text{for all } x \in
U_0.
\end{equation*}
 
By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, there exists a regular map $\beta \colon \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^n$ such that the restriction $\beta|_{U_0}$ is arbitrarily close to the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $\eta_1 \colon U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $x \mapsto \eta(x,1)$ in the $\mathcal{C}^0$ topology. Then
 
\begin{equation*}
    \alpha \colon U \to \mathbb{R}^k \times Y, \quad x \mapsto s(F(x,0), \beta(x))
\end{equation*}
 
is a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ section of $h \colon \mathbb{R}^k \times Y \to \mathbb{R}^k$ such that $\alpha|_{U_0}$ is close in the $\mathcal{C}^0$ topology to the section
 
\begin{equation*}
    U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^k \times Y, \quad x \mapsto (x, \psi(x)).
\end{equation*}
 
We have $\alpha(x) = (x, \theta(x))$, where $\theta \colon U \to Y$ is a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map. Since $F(x,0) = (x, \varphi(x))$ and $\varphi|_X = \gamma$ is a regular map, the restriction $g \coloneqq \theta|_X \colon X \to Y$ is a regular map. By construction, $g|_{X \cap U_0}$ is close to the continuous map $\psi|_{X \cap U_0} = f|_{X \cap U_0}$. The proof is complete since $U_0$ is chosen in an arbitrary way.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop-2-8}, the variety $Y$ is malleable. Hence the
conclusion follows from Theorems \ref{th-4-2} and \ref{th-4-3}.

label: th-4-4
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{th-1-1}, \ref{th-4-4-a} implies \ref{th-4-4-b}. To prove
the reversed implication suppose that \ref{th-4-4-a} does not hold.
Then, by Chevalley's theorem \cite{bib25} (see \cite{bib26} for a modern
treatment), there exists a surjective morphism of algebraic $\mathbb{R}$-groups
$\varphi \colon \Gamma \to A$, where $A$ is an Abelian $\mathbb{R}$-variety,
$\dim A \geq 1$. Since $\varphi$ is defined over $\mathbb{R}$, its restriction
$\varphi(\mathbb{R}) \colon \Gamma(\mathbb{R}) \to A(\mathbb{R})$ is a regular map of real
algebraic varieties. The image $\varphi(\mathbb{R})(\Gamma(\mathbb{R}))$ is Zariski
dense in $A(\mathbb{R})$, the map $\varphi$ being surjective. Hence there exists
a point $a \in \Gamma(\mathbb{R})$ at which the derivative $d_a \varphi(\mathbb{R})
\colon T_a\Gamma(\mathbb{R}) \to T_{\varphi(\mathbb{R})(a)}A(\mathbb{R})$ is surjective.
Therefore, in view of the rank theorem for $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps, we can find a
continuous null homotopic map $f \colon \mathbb{S}^k \to \Gamma(\mathbb{R})$ such that
the composite map $\varphi(\mathbb{R}) \circ f \colon \mathbb{S}^k \to A(\mathbb{R})$ is not
constant. It follows that $\varphi(\mathbb{R}) \circ f$ cannot be approximated
by regular maps in the $\mathcal{C}^0$ topology because each regular map from
$\mathbb{S}^k$ into $A(\mathbb{R})$ is constant, see \cite[Corollary~3.9]{bib52}.
Consequently, \ref{th-4-4-b} does not hold. In other words,
\ref{th-4-4-b} implies \ref{th-4-4-a}.

label: th-5-1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-5-1}
Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented nonsingular real algebraic
variety of dimension $n$. Then the set of regular maps $\mathcal{R}(X, \mathbb{S}^n)$
is dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(X, \mathbb{S}^n)$ if and only
if there exists a regular map from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^n$ of topological
degree~$1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $f \colon X \to \mathbb{S}^n$ is a regular map with $\deg(f)=1$.
By \cite[Corollary~4.2]{bib4}, for every integer $d$ there exists a
regular map $\varphi_d \colon \mathbb{S}^n \to \mathbb{S}^n$ with $\deg(\varphi_d)=d$.
Since the composite map $\varphi_d \circ f$ is regular and
$\deg(\varphi_d \circ f) = d$, it follows from Hopf's theorem that each
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^n$ is homotopic to a regular map.
Therefore the set $\mathcal{R}(X, \mathbb{S}^n)$ is dense in the space $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(X,
\mathbb{S}^n)$ by Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}. The converse is obvious.
head: environment

label: ex-5-2
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-5-2}
Let $n,k$ be two positive integers and let $\mathbb{S}^n_{2k}$ be the Fermat
$n$-sphere of degree $2k$,
 
\begin{equation*}
\mathbb{S}^n_{2k} = \{(x_0,\ldots,x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} : x_0^{2k} + \cdots +
x_n^{2k} = 1\}.
\end{equation*}
 
Clearly, $\mathbb{S}^n_{2k}$ is a nonsingular real algebraic variety
diffeomorphic to the unit $n$-sphere ${\mathbb{S}^n=\mathbb{S}^n_2}$. If $k$ is odd, then
the set of regular maps $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^n_{2k}, \mathbb{S}^n)$ is dense in the space
of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^n_{2k}, \mathbb{S}^n)$. Indeed, the regular map
 
\begin{equation*}
f \colon \mathbb{S}^n_{2k} \to \mathbb{S}^n, \quad (x_0, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto (x_0^k,
\ldots, x_n^k)
\end{equation*}
 
is a homeomorphism, and hence $\deg(f) = 1$ if $\mathbb{S}^n_{2k}$ is oriented
in the standard way. Therefore the assertion follows from
Theorem~\ref{th-5-1}.\qed
head: environment

label: th-5-3
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Hopf's theorem, there are exactly two homotopic classes of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$
maps from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^n$. One of them is represented by a constant map
(which obviously is a regular map). Therefore the proof is complete in
view of Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}.
head: environment

label: ex-5-4
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-5-4}
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let $X_k$ be the blowup of the
$2$-sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$ at $k$~points. Clearly, $X_k$ is a compact connected
nonsingular real algebraic surface, which is a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ nonorientable
surface of genus $k$. According to \cite[Theorem~1.7]{bib3}, the set
$\mathcal{R}(X_k, \mathbb{S}^2)$ is dense in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(X_k, \mathbb{S}^2)$ for all $k \geq 1$.
Furthermore, if $k$ is odd, then for every algebraic model~$X$ of $X_k$
the set $\mathcal{R}(X, \mathbb{S}^2)$ is dense in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(X, \mathbb{S}^2)$ by
\cite[Theorem~2]{bib5}. However, if $k$ is even, then there exists an
algebraic model~$Y$ of $X_k$ such that the closure of $\mathcal{R}(Y,\mathbb{S}^2)$ in
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(Y, \mathbb{S}^2)$ consists precisely of all $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ null homotopic
maps from Y into $\mathbb{S}^2$, see \cite[Theorem~3.3]{bib5}.
head: environment

label: prop-5-5
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f \colon \mathbb{S}^n \to Y$ be a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map. Choose an element $a \in
G$ such that $a \cdot f(s_n)=y_0$. Since $\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_n(Y,y_0) =
\pi_n(Y,y_0)$, the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $g \colon \mathbb{S}^n \to Y$, $x \mapsto a
\cdot f(x)$ is homotopic to a regular map, and hence, by
Theorem~\ref{th-1-1}, it can be approximated by regular maps in the
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology. Consequently, the map $f$ can be approximated by
regular maps in the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ topology because $f(x) = a^{-1} \cdot g(x)$
for all $x \in \mathbb{S}^n$.
head: environment

label: th-5-6
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-5-6}
Let $(n,p)$ be a pair of positive integers. Then the set of regular maps
$\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^n,\mathbb{S}^p)$ is dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^n,\mathbb{S}^p)$ in each of the following five cases:
 
\begin{iconditions}
\item\label{th-5-6-i} $p=1,2$ or $4$.

\item\label{th-5-6-ii} $n-p \leq 3$.

\item\label{th-5-6-iii} $4 \leq n-p \leq 5$ with possible exception for
the pairs $(9,5)$, $(7,3)$, $(11,6)$, $(10,5)$ and $(8,3)$.

\item\label{th-5-6-iv} The homotopy group $\pi_n(\mathbb{S}^p)$ is finite
cyclic of odd order, and $p$ is odd with $n \leq 2p-2$.

\item\label{th-5-6-v} $n=p+13$, where $p$ is odd and $p \geq 15$.
\end{iconditions}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{th-5-6-i} This is proved in \cite[Theorem~1.1]{bib3}
and has already been mentioned in Section~\ref{sec:1}.

\ref{th-5-6-ii} The case $n=p$ is contained in Theorem~\ref{th-1-6}. For
$1 \leq n-p \leq 3$, one has $\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_n(\mathbb{S}^p) = \pi_n(\mathbb{S}^p)$ by
\cite[Corollaries 1.2, 1.3  and 1.4]{bib56}. The case $n<p$ is trivial.

\ref{th-5-6-iii} One has $\pi_{p+4}(\mathbb{S}^p)=0$ for $p \geq 6$ and
$\pi_{p+5}(\mathbb{S}^p)=0$ for $p \geq 7$ (see \cite[\mbox{pp. 331, 332}]{bib35}), which
together with \ref{th-5-6-i} completes the proof.

\ref{th-5-6-iv} In this case, $\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_n(\mathbb{S}^p) = \pi_n(\mathbb{S}^p)$ by
\cite[Theorem~2.1 and p.~163]{bib4}.

\ref{th-5-6-v} One has $\pi_{p+13}(\mathbb{S}^p) = \mathbb{Z}/3$ if $p \geq 15$ (see
\cite[p.~188]{bib59}), so the assertion follows from~\ref{th-5-6-iv}.

label: prop-5-7
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-5-7}
Let $Y$ be either a real algebraic group or the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^7$.
Then, for every positive integer~$n$, the subset $\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_n(Y)$ is a
subgroup of the homotopy group $\pi_n(Y)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the case under consideration, the H-space multiplication $Y \times Y
\to Y$, $(a,b) \mapsto ab$ and the inverse operation $Y \to Y$, $a
\mapsto a^{-1}$ are regular maps. The assertion follows since the group
operation in $\pi_n(Y)$ is induced by the H-space multiplication.
head: environment

label: ex-5-8
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-5-8}
Let $(n,p)$ be a pair of integers, $n>p\geq 1$. Then there exist an
algebraic model $X$ of the $n$-dimensional torus $(\mathbb{S}^1)^n$ and a
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $f \colon X \to \mathbb{S}^p$ such that $f$ is not homotopic to
any regular map from $X$ into $\mathbb{S}^p$.

This assertion can be proved as follows. Let $h \colon (\mathbb{S}^1)^p \to
\mathbb{S}^p$ be a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map of topological degree~$1$. Then the induced
homomorphism in homology ${h_* \colon H_p((\mathbb{S}^1)^p; \mathbb{Z}/2) \to H_p(\mathbb{S}^p;
\mathbb{Z}/2)}$ is an isomorphism. Let $w$ be a generator of the cohomology group
$H^p(\mathbb{S}^p; \mathbb{Z}/2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$; so $w$~corresponds via the Poincar\'e
duality to a point in $\mathbb{S}^p$. Clearly, if $[(\mathbb{S}^1)^p] \in
H_p((\mathbb{S}^1)^p; \mathbb{Z}/2)$ is the fundamental class of $(\mathbb{S}^1)^p$, then the
Kronecker index $\langle w, h_*([(\mathbb{S}^1)^p])\rangle$ is nonzero.
Therefore the assertion holds by \cite[Theorem~2.8]{bib16} (with
$K=(\mathbb{S}^1)^p$, $L=(\mathbb{S}^1)^{n-p}$, $Y=\mathbb{S}^p$).

Consequently, the set of regular maps
$\mathcal{R}(X, \mathbb{S}^p)$ is not dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(X,
\mathbb{S}^p)$.

label: ex-5-9
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-5-9}
The results depend strongly on the specific values of $p$ and $q$. In
what follows by a degree of a map we mean a topological degree.
 
\begin{exconditions}[widest=iii]
\item\label{ex-5-9-i} According to \cite[Theorem~12]{bib50}, there
exists a regular map $\mathbb{S}^4 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \to \mathbb{S}^6$ of degree~$1$.
Hence, in view of \cite[Corollary~4.2]{bib4}, for every integer~$d$
there exists a regular map ${\mathbb{S}^4 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \to \mathbb{S}^6}$ of degree~$d$.
Now, it follows from Hopf's theorem that each $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $\mathbb{S}^4
\times \mathbb{S}^2 \to \mathbb{S}^6$ is homotopic to a regular map. Consequently, by
Corollary~\ref{cor-1-5}, the set of regular maps $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^4 \times
\mathbb{S}^2, \mathbb{S}^6)$ is dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^4
\times \mathbb{S}^2, \mathbb{S}^6)$.

\item\label{ex-5-9-ii} The same argument shows that $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^4 \times
\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{S}^5)$ is dense in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^4 \times \mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{S}^5)$.


\item\label{ex-5-9-iii} By \cite[Theorem~14]{bib50} and
\cite[Corollary~4.2]{bib4}, for every even integer~$d$ there exists a
regular map $\mathbb{S}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \to \mathbb{S}^4$ of degree~$d$. It is an open
problem whether there exists a regular map $\mathbb{S}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \to
\mathbb{S}^4$ of odd degree; if it does, then $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^2, \mathbb{S}^4)$
is dense in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^2, \mathbb{S}^4)$.

\item\label{ex-5-9-iv} Assuming that both $p$ and $q$ are odd positive
integers, according to Theorem~\ref{th-1-7}, a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ map $f \colon
\mathbb{S}^p \times \mathbb{S}^q \to \mathbb{S}^{p+q}$ can be approximated by regular maps if
and only if it is null homotopic.
\end{exconditions}

label: prop-6-1
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
According to Bott's periodicity theorem \cite{bib21} (see also
\cite[Chap.~8, Remark~4.2, and~12.2]{bib36}) the $n$th homotopy group
$\pi_n(Y)$ is trivial in cases \ref{prop-6-1-i}, \ref{prop-6-1-ii} and
\ref{prop-6-1-iii}. Furthermore, by \cite[Chap.~8, Theorem~5.1]{bib36},
the homotopy group $\pi_n(Y)$ is trivial in case \ref{prop-6-1-iv}.
Therefore the proof is complete in view of Corollary~\ref{cor-1-2}.
head: environment

label: th-6-2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-6-2}
Let $(n,m)$ be a pair of positive integers and let $G(m)$ denote either
$\mathrm{U}(m)$ or $\mathrm{SU}(m)$. Assume that $n=2k-1$ is odd and $m \geq 2^{k-1}$.
Then the set of regular maps $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^n, G(m))$ is dense in the space of
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^n, G(m))$.

label: c1
title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop-5-5}, it is sufficient to show that
$\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_{2k-1}(G(m)) = \pi_{2k-1}(G(m))$.

\begin{case}\label{c1}
Suppose that $(k,m) = (1,m)$ with $m\geq 1$. It is well known that
${\pi_1(\mathrm{SU}(m)) = 0}$, and the inclusion map $\mathrm{U}(1) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{U}(m)$
induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(\mathrm{U}(1)) \cong \pi_1(U(m))$. Case~\ref{c1}
follows since $\mathrm{U}(1) = \mathbb{S}^1$ and $\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_1(\mathbb{S}^1)=\pi_1(\mathbb{S}^1)$.
\end{case}

\begin{case}\label{c2}
Suppose that $k \geq 2$ and $m \geq 2^{k-1}$. The inclusion map
$G(2^{k-1}) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{2^{k-1}}(\mathbb{C})$ induces an isomorphism
of the homotopy groups $\pi_{2k-1}(G(2^{k-1}))$ and
$\pi_{2k-1}(\mathrm{GL}_{2^{k-1}}(\mathbb{C}))$. As explained above, the latter group is
generated by the homotopy class represented by the map $a_k$. Since
$a_k$ is a regular map with values in $G(2^{k-1})$, we get
$\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_{2k-1}(G(2^{k-1})) = \pi_{2k-1}(G(2^{k-1}))$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop-5-7}. Moreover, the inclusion map $G(2^{k-1})
\hookrightarrow G(m)$ induces an isomorphism of the homotopy groups
$\pi_{2k-1}(G(2^{k-1}))$ and $\pi_{2k-1}(G(m))$ (see \cite[Chap.~8, Remark~4.2]{bib36}), and hence $\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_{2k-1}(G(m)) =
\pi_{2k-1}(G(m))$.\qedhere
\end{case}

label: prop-6-3
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-6-3}
Let $(n,m)$ be a pair of positive integers and let $G(m)$ denote either
$\mathrm{U}(m)$ or $\mathrm{SU}(m)$. Assume that $1 \leq n \leq 6$. Then the set of
regular maps $\mathcal{R}(\mathbb{S}^n, G(m))$ is dense in the space of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ maps
$\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^n, G(m))$, possibly with the exception of $(n,m)=(5,3)$ or
$(n,m)=(6,3)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $(n,m)\neq(5,3)$ and $(n,m)\neq(6,3)$. Then the only cases
not already covered by Proposition~\ref{prop-6-1} and
Theorem~\ref{th-6-2} are $(n,m)$ equal to $(4,2)$, $(5,2)$ and $(6,2)$.
Hence, by Proposition~\ref{prop-5-5}, it is sufficient to show that
$\pi^{\mathrm{alg}}_n(G(2)) = \pi_n(G(2))$ for $n=4,5$ and~$6$. This is proved in
\cite[Corollaries~1.2, 1.3 and 1.4]{bib56} for $G(2)=\mathrm{SU}(2)=\mathbb{S}^3$. The
case $G(2)=\mathrm{U}(2)$ follows since the inclusion map $\mathrm{SU}(m)
\hookrightarrow \mathrm{U}(m)$ induces for all $i \geq 2$ an isomorphism between
the corresponding $i$th homotopy groups, see \cite[Chap.~8,
12.2]{bib36}.

name: Proof using Chevalley's theorem

body_md:
We use the Iwasawa decomposition to write
$G=K\times (\mathbb{R}^\times)^r\times U$
where $K$ is compact and $U$ is unipotent. 

The Lie algebra $L_U$ of $U$ is nilpotent, so the exponential map
$\exp\colon L_U\to U$ is algebraic and even a homeomorphism. 
The $\mathbb{R}^\times$ factor is the least natural, but we can use
$g\colon \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}^\times$ given by $t\mapsto (1+t+t^2)(1+t^2)^{-1}$.

It remains to deal with $K$. For any root $\alpha$ we have a subgroup
 $\mathbb{S}^1\cong C_\alpha\subset K$.  Composing it with the inverse of the
 stereographic projection from $-1$   we get
$g_\alpha\colon \mathbb{R}^1\to \mathbb{S}^1\cong C_\alpha\subset K$.

Now fix an ordering of the roots and send
$v=\sum c_\alpha \alpha$ to
 
\begin{equation*}
    \pushQED{\qed}
    g(v)\coloneqq\textstyle{\prod}_{\alpha} g_\alpha(c_\alpha)\in K. \qedhere
    \popQED
\end{equation*}
 
Note that $g$ does depend on the ordering of the roots. It would be interesting to find a more natural construction that generalizes the Cayley transform.

name: Proof using Chevalley's method

title: Example
body_md:
Let $A$ be a skew-symmetric $n\times n$ matrix.  Then $I + A$ is invertible, and the Cayley transform is
$ Q(A)\coloneqq(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$.
Then $Q(A)$ is  an orthogonal matrix, giving the required map
$Q\colon T_0\mathrm{SO}_n\to \mathrm{SO}_n$.

Similarly, starting with a skew-Hermitian matrix $A$  we get
$Q\colon T_0\mathrm{U}_n\to \mathrm{U}_n$.
